title: What's your stack for running a trading agent?
author: Money_Horror_2899
selftext:
Curious to get a picture of where traders are at when it comes to agentic trading.

Poll options:

1. Python + a broker or exchange API
2. TradingView alerts + webhooks
3. Open-source framework (Freqtrade, TradingAgents, LEAN...)
4. No-code platforms (Obside, Composer, Capitalise...)
5. An LLM chat, and I place the orders myself
6. Nothing running yet

In the comments: the stage you are at (backtest, paper, live), and the one thing that breaks most often.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
Python against a broker's data API, and everything I run sits at the paper stage on purpose, because that's where the real breakage shows up.

What breaks most isn't the strategy logic, it's time. A bar that lands a few seconds late, a half day before a holiday, the open shifting an hour in UTC when the clocks change. The rule fires on the wrong candle, and the backtest never warned you because the backtest had perfect clocks.

Quantradin came out of exactly that gap. I built it to run a rule, or your AI over MCP, on fake money with real prices and no look-ahead, free, so the timing bugs show up before any money does.

comments.author: Zealou-sidealIron
comments.body: The point about time and timezone shifts is spot on. Backtests assume flawless clocks and instant data delivery, but live infrastructure deals with network jitter, API rate limits, and daylight saving discrepancies that completely throw off execution timing

comments.author: DanklyNight
comments.body:
1. Mix of Python/Rust, we built the trading engine over many years of hard work to ensure we are accurate down to a millisecond across backtest/paper/live. Backtest is accurate about 98% to live and paper is 99.98% accurate.

We pull in essentially every data source possible live and hold it historically also.

2. Our own events system, ideas get turned into events.

3. Fully close sourced built by us from the ground up, I imagine there are some components of the engine that are around 10 years old by this point.

  
Live on strategies fully built by agents from the ground up, we have executed well over 7 figures in total.

We may be an outlier, but we are also running B300's and RTX 6000 Pros + own all of the underlying infrastructure so we can be extremely tight on what we are doing.

  
I think that's about as much as I can give away 😄

comments.author: Skye_Figer
comments.body:
I ended up building my own platform. Currently running backtests, paper trading, and small live tests.

The core is a custom data ingestion pipeline and a unified trading engine across all three modes, covering roughly 11,000 symbols at minute resolution. Data stack is S3/Parquet for historical storage, ClickHouse for queries, Redis for live caching, and Postgres for application and transaction data.

The agent side connects through MCP, so Claude can research, configure strategies, run backtests, and handle some account management. The configured strategy rules run through the deterministic trading engine, with human approval before promoting a strategy to live.

The hardest part has been getting backtest, paper, and live behavior to line up—and being able to explain the differences when they don’t. For example, a strategy in a shared paper account can skip a trade because another strategy used the available buying power, while an isolated backtest takes it. Same rules, different account conditions.

I’ve put a lot of work into audit logs so I can trace why a trade happened or was skipped. That’s been essential for figuring out whether a mismatch is a bug, a data issue, or an expected difference in execution conditions.
